The Story

A girl who draws life,
teaches language, and
dreams of the sea.

I have lived in Laos for 11 years — longer than I've lived anywhere else. My parents chose service over stability, and I grew up watching that choice shape everything our family values.

Two things have stayed with me for as long as I can remember: I draw constantly, and I am fascinated by living creatures. At seven I sculpted clay dogs by the boxful. At fifteen I animated a short film frame by frame. Today I fill sketchbooks with animals and study the biology behind them. My art teacher and I have begun talking seriously about scientific illustration as a career path — the place where biological accuracy and visual craft meet.

I also want to work in aquariums. Not as a casual interest, but as a professional goal — in education, exhibit design, or conservation communication. This portfolio documents the experiences that make that goal legible.

🐠 Aquarium Professional (Goal)

Aspiring to work in public aquarium education or conservation communication — where science, art, and public engagement converge.

🎨 Visual Artist & Illustrator

6+ portfolio pieces, 1:30 self-directed animation, clay sculpture, prop-making. Art classes twice weekly. Exploring scientific illustration as a formal direction.

🗣️ Educator Across Languages

Designed and taught a Hangul curriculum for Lao kindergarteners. Official Korean-Lao interpreter for 3 education missions in Xieng Khouang Province.

🌏 Missionary Kid, Global Thinker

11 years in Laos shaped how I see service, sacrifice, and the responsibility to communicate across every barrier — cultural, linguistic, and scientific.

Section A

Aquariums &
the Living World

My interest in aquariums is not decorative. I want to work in one — in education, exhibit design, or animal care communication. Growing up landlocked in Laos created a curiosity about marine life that proximity alone never could.

I'm actively exploring what that path looks like — including the possibility of an aquarium internship while still in high school. My goal is a degree that bridges biology and visual communication, aimed at careers where science education meets the public.

🐠 Coral Reef Ecology 🐋 Marine Mammals 🦑 Cephalopods 🌿 Seagrass Systems 🔬 Bioluminescence 🌊 Ocean Conservation

"I draw animals because I love them. I want to work where that love is useful — in a place that cares for living things and teaches the public why they matter."

Scientific illustration sits exactly where my interests converge: biological accuracy, visual craft, and public communication. Whether that leads to aquarium education, natural history publishing, or conservation animation — I intend to find out.

Section C

Three Languages,
One Identity

I was born Korean. I was raised Lao. I was educated in English. Each language gave me a different way of seeing the world — and a different way of explaining it to others.

For a future marine biologist and science communicator, this is not background noise. It is the core competency. The ability to make complex ideas comprehensible across languages, cultures, and contexts is exactly what the ocean needs from its advocates.

"I grew up between three languages — Korean, Lao, and English. And somewhere in the silence between them, I found my voice."

— Common App Essay theme · "Three Languages" narrative

Program 2

Interpreter Mission,
Xieng Khouang

Xieng Khouang is a remote province in northern Laos — hours from the capital, with few resources and even fewer outside visitors. Since 2023, I have joined a Korean church mission team to Xieng Khouang three times (2023, 2024, 2025), serving as the sole Korean-Lao interpreter.

Each mission was based at Somvatthana School. Over 3–7 days on-site, I interpreted between Korean team members and Lao school staff and students — enabling classroom instruction, school events, and community activities. The role demanded cultural sensitivity, real-time judgment, and the ability to make both sides feel genuinely heard.

Across three trips, I contributed approximately 60 hours of active service. The school issued an official verification letter in Lao — rare documentation that formally confirms this role.

Looking Forward

What Laos Taught Me
About the Ocean

01

Ecosystems Need Translators

The ocean's crisis is partly a communication crisis. Scientists know what's happening. But the people who can change it don't always speak the language. I grew up being that bridge — and I intend to keep building it.

02

Distance Creates Depth

Being landlocked made me love the ocean more, not less. Absence sharpened my attention. The same is true for science communication: the best explainers are not always insiders. Sometimes they're people who had to seek it out.

03

Service Is the Method

My family chose to live with less so others could have more. That orientation — service as a way of being, not just doing — is the foundation of both conservation science and community education. I don't know another way.

Jueun Jang · Marine Biologist in Training · Vientiane, Laos · 2023–2026

Built with care, for the ocean
